title: TA9-03315
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Nigeria. He seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). 1 ALLEGATIONS

In 2004 the claimant was hired, on a contractual basis, by the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, to collect information on former Delta State Governor, XXXXX XXXX, who was being investigated by the Commission with respect to alleged money laundering and embezzlement of public funds.

The claimant then proceeded to collect incriminating information on XXXXX XXXX, which he subsequently submitted to XXXX Director, XXXXX XXXX, through XXXXX XXXX, an XXXX employee, who was directly supervising the work of the claimant. After XXXXX XXXX was removed from his position, the claimant started getting strange calls and death threats from one XXXXX XXXX, an agent of XXXXX XXXX. XXXXX XXXX vowed to kill the claimant for his role in bringing charges of corruption against XXXXX XXXX.

In XXXXX 2008, the claimant was shot at while in a friend's car, but managed to escape. Believing his identity had been compromised, and having received no support from the police in his home town of XXXX, the claimant went into hiding in XXXX. While in XXXX, the claimant was once again discovered, and XXXXX XXXX, his supervisor at XXXX, was killed, while both were out together for the evening. Believing that his life was in danger, the claimant fled to Lagos where arrangements were then made for his flight to Canada.
The Panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor is he a person in need of protection in accordance with section 97(1)(a) and (b) of the IRPA. ANALYSIS Identity

The claimant produced a number of documents corroborating his identity.2 The Panel is persuaded, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is who he says he is, and a citizen of Nigeria. Credibility

The claimant indicated in his Personal Information Form (PIF)3 that he had begun work as an administrative assistant in his uncle's private investigation business, but quickly learned the business, working primarily "for clients who sought to find out about their partner's infidelity...and for clients who sought to know if their employees were stealing from them."4 He was then, allegedly, offered a job by the Director of the EFCC to gather incriminating information on the then Governor of Delta State, XXXXX XXXX. The Panel finds it implausible that the Director of a high profile national agency would hire a 25 year old inexperienced private investigator, whose experience essentially was made up of spying on cheating spouses and dishonest employees, to investigate a senior government official suspected of committing major fraud and misuse of public funds.

The claimant produced a letter from the XXXX signed by XXXXXX XXXX, Head of the Forensic Unit, who was killed shortly afterwards. The letter indicated that the claimant was authorized to conduct inquiries with respect to Chief XXXXX XXXX and Agencies of the Federal Government of Nigeria.5 The letter, however, does not provide any dates as to when the claimant actually performed these duties on behalf of the XXXX or the period he was employed by the XXXX. The letter itself does not appear to be authentic. The XXXX logo on the letter appears to be cut off at the top, and is visibly different from the logo as it appears both in an article in one of the claimant's exhibits,6 as well as, on XXXX official website.7 The address line in the letterhead has the city of XXXX XXXXX spelled with the "h" in lowercase as opposed to uppercase, as it appears in official references to the city.8 The claimant's counsel argued that the problems with the letter are simply a reflection of the lower standards in Nigeria with respect to documents as compared to more developed countries. The Panel is not persuaded that a national agency such as the XXXX would not care about, or be able to ensure the quality of its official stationary. In light of the problems outlined, the Panel concludes that the letter is not authentic. As the only evidence that corroborates the claimant's allegation that he was employed by the XXXX to investigate XXXXX XXXX is found, on a balance of probabilities, to be fraudulent, the Panel must also discount the claimant's assertion that the problems he encountered in Nigeria were as a result of his investigation of XXXX XXXX, while under contract to XXXX.

As well, if indeed the XXXX Director, XXXXX XXXX, had concerns with having his staff investigate XXXXX XXXX, he could have turned to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID)9 of the Nigerian Police, who conduct investigations into fraud, as opposed to relying on an inexperienced person, like the claimant, to do the work.

The claimant further indicated that an attempt was made on his life by men who shot at him while he was in his friend's car, and that this action was a direct result of his investigation of XXXX XXXX. When the claimant reported the incident to the police, they advised him that the men who attacked him were likely armed robbers.

Because of the existence of credibility issues in areas central and material to the claim, the Panel does not find the claimant to be a credible witness, and ultimately, for all the reasons discussed, does not accept the claimant's written narrative or oral testimony with respect to the events which formed the basis of his claim.

In light of the issues around credibility and the claimant's inability to provide any persuasive evidence to support his allegations, the Panel is unable to conclude that the attack on the claimant was anything other than a criminal act. Therefore, the Panel determines that there is no nexus to any of the Convention grounds, and finds that there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if he were returned to Nigeria Section 97: Risk of Harm

The claimant has not demonstrated that, it is more likely than not, that he would face a risk to life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture if he were to return Nigeria. There was no persuasive evidence, that the attack in XXXX was anything other than, as the police concluded, an act of criminality.

Further, no evidence was presented to allow the Panel to conclude that the subsequent shooting of XXXXX XXXX in XXXXX, in anyway, involved the claimant, or that he was also targeted. When XXXXX XXXX was shot and killed, the claimant was in the washroom at the time. One would have expected assassins to have struck either before or after the claimant left to go to the washroom if in fact he was also being targeted. The Panel must then conclude that if the claimant were to return to Nigeria, he would not be subjected to an individualized risk of harm under section 97(1). Therefore, the claimant has not demonstrated, on a balance of probabilities, that he would face harm under section 97(1) of IRPA if he were to return to Nigeria.

The Panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
